title: Ezekiel 24:1–14
context: The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel in the ninth year, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month. The prophet, addressed as “son of man,” is told to write the name of that same day: the king of Babylon drew close to Jerusalem this same day. 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52 also tell of the king of Babylon coming against Jerusalem in the ninth year, in the tenth month; this oracle is dated to that same day and is not merged with those narratives. The Lord GOD then gives a parable to the rebellious house: a cauldron is set on the fire, filled with water and with the choice pieces and bones of the flock, and made to boil well. The pot is “the bloody city,” a cauldron whose rust has not gone out of it; the pieces are taken out one after another, and no lots are cast. The blood she shed is left on the bare rock, uncovered, so that wrath may come up to take vengeance. The fire is made hotter still, the pot is set empty on its coals, and the bronze is to burn until the rust is consumed. The city has been weary with toil, yet the rust does not leave her. The LORD says he had cleansed her, and she was not cleansed; she will not be cleansed from her filthiness until his wrath toward her rests. The LORD has spoken, and it will happen; he will not go back. The cauldron is the sign of a city under siege and under judgment, told as a cooking scene and not as a spectacle.

verses.text: Again, in the ninth year, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Again, in the ninth year, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, the LORD’s word came to me, saying,” Ezekiel dates the word with care. The speaker of the report is the prophet; the word is the LORD’s. The same ninth year and tenth month appear in the siege accounts of 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 52, and those records stand beside this heading without being blended into one line.

Arminian readers take the date as a real day in the prophet’s life, a word that arrives when the city is about to be closed in, and that Israel can still hear as a living address.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same heading as the LORD’s word, timed to the day, a dated speech and not a later guess about the siege.

Shared ground: the oracle is fixed to this ninth year, tenth month, and tenth day. The traditions read the date together.

verses.text: “Son of man, write the name of the day, this same day. The king of Babylon drew close to Jerusalem this same day.
verses.arminianNotes:
The prophet is addressed as “Son of man,” the book’s ordinary title for him, and is told, “write the name of the day, this same day. The king of Babylon drew close to Jerusalem this same day.” The parable that follows is tied to an event already underway: Babylon’s king has drawn close, and the day is to be written down.

Arminian readers hear a command to record the day because the approach is real, a public fact the prophet is not to let slip, and a word the house can still receive as warning and as truth.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same title and the same command: the day is named because the LORD says the king of Babylon has drawn close to Jerusalem on it.

Shared ground: “this same day” is the hinge of the chapter’s first movement. The title “son of man” is the prophet’s address, not a dispute about another figure.

verses.text: Utter a parable to the rebellious house, and tell them, ‘The Lord GOD says, “Put the cauldron on the fire. Put it on, and also pour water into it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezekiel is told, “Utter a parable to the rebellious house,” and the Lord GOD says, “Put the cauldron on the fire. Put it on, and also pour water into it.” The rebellious house is the audience. The picture begins simply: a pot on the fire, with water in it, ready for what will be gathered next.

Arminian readers take the parable as a word aimed at a house that has resisted, a cooking sign they can understand, and a call that still meets them as hearers of the Lord GOD.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same parable as the Lord GOD’s own opening: the cauldron is set on, and water is poured in, the first move of a judgment already in motion.

Shared ground: the pot on the fire is the beginning of the sign. The house is called rebellious, and both traditions receive that charge as the oracle’s own.

verses.text: Gather its pieces into it, even every good piece: the thigh and the shoulder. Fill it with the choice bones.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Gather its pieces into it, even every good piece: the thigh and the shoulder. Fill it with the choice bones.” The pot is filled with the good pieces and the choice bones. Many readers take the pieces as the people of the city, gathered into the vessel that will now boil; the oracle itself has not yet named the pot as the city, and that reading waits on the “bloody city” of the next movement.

Arminian readers hear a gathering of what seems choice and good, all of it placed in the pot, a sign that even what looks choice is not outside the fire.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same filling of the cauldron with thigh, shoulder, and choice bones as the Lord GOD’s appointed picture of those gathered in the city.

Shared ground: every good piece is gathered in. The image is a cooking pot, told plainly, without added gore.

verses.text: Take the choice of the flock, and also a pile of wood for the bones under the cauldron. Make it boil well. Yes, let its bones be boiled within it.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Take the choice of the flock, and also a pile of wood for the bones under the cauldron. Make it boil well. Yes, let its bones be boiled within it.” The choice of the flock goes in, wood is piled under the bones, and the boiling is to be thorough, even to the bones. The sign is a pot made to boil well, a siege and a judgment that will not be a light simmer.

Arminian readers hear the command to make it boil well as a real warning to the rebellious house: the fire under the pot will do its work, and the word still meets them as a word they can hear.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the piled wood, the choice of the flock, and the bones boiled within the pot as the Lord GOD’s own description of a thorough boiling.

Shared ground: the pot is made to boil well. The cooking language stays the language of the sign, not a scene to be enlarged.

verses.text: “ ‘Therefore the Lord GOD says: “Woe to the bloody city, to the cauldron whose rust is in it, and whose rust hasn’t gone out of it! Take out of it piece after piece without casting lots for it.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Woe to the bloody city, to the cauldron whose rust is in it, and whose rust hasn’t gone out of it!” The pot is now named: the bloody city, a cauldron with rust still in it. “Take out of it piece after piece without casting lots for it.” The pieces come out one after another, and no lots are cast. Many readers take that to mean no one is selected for escape by lot; the verse itself simply says the pieces are taken out without lots.

Arminian readers hear a woe over a city whose stain has not gone out, and a removal of piece after piece, a judgment that does not pretend to a lucky exemption.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same woe, the rust that has not gone out, and the taking of piece after piece without lots, as the Lord GOD’s word over the bloody city.

Shared ground: the cauldron is the bloody city, and its rust remains. That identification is the oracle’s own.

verses.text: “ ‘ “For the blood she shed is in the middle of her. She set it on the bare rock. She didn’t pour it on the ground, to cover it with dust.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For the blood she shed is in the middle of her. She set it on the bare rock. She didn’t pour it on the ground, to cover it with dust.” The city’s bloodshed is left in the open, on bare rock, not covered with dust as spilled blood might be covered on the ground. The image is of guilt left uncovered, told in that plain way and not turned into a spectacle.

Arminian readers hear a charge of blood left visible, a violence the city did not hide, and a reason the coming wrath is not without a cause they can recognize.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the blood in the middle of her, set on the bare rock and not covered with dust, as the Lord GOD’s account of uncovered guilt.

Shared ground: the blood is not covered. The sign stays a sign of open bloodshed, spoken with restraint.

verses.text: That it may cause wrath to come up to take vengeance, I have set her blood on the bare rock, that it should not be covered.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The uncovered blood is also the LORD’s doing: “I have set her blood on the bare rock,” so that it is not covered, and so that wrath may come up to take vengeance. The city’s open guilt and the LORD’s exposing of it stand together in the one line.

Arminian readers hear a vengeance that answers visible blood, a wrath that rises because the stain was left in the open, and a word that still addresses the house about what it has done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same setting of the blood on the bare rock, uncovered, as the LORD’s act, so that wrath comes up to take vengeance.

Shared ground: the blood is on the bare rock, and wrath rises to take vengeance. Both traditions hear the LORD in that exposing.

verses.text: “ ‘Therefore the Lord GOD says: “Woe to the bloody city! I also will make the pile great.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Woe to the bloody city! I also will make the pile great.” The woe is spoken again, and the LORD will make the pile of fuel great. The fire already under the pot will not be a small fire.

Arminian readers hear a second woe, and a pile made great, a warning that the judgment will be ample, still spoken to a house that can hear the woe as woe.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the repeated woe and the great pile as the Lord GOD’s own resolve to enlarge the fire under the city.

Shared ground: the bloody city is addressed again, and the pile will be great. The traditions do not divide over this second woe.

verses.text: Heap on the wood. Make the fire hot. Boil the meat well. Make the broth thick, and let the bones be burned.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Heap on the wood. Make the fire hot. Boil the meat well. Make the broth thick, and let the bones be burned.” The commands pile up: more wood, a hotter fire, meat boiled well, broth made thick, bones burned. The thoroughness of the boiling is the point of the sign, and the language stays that of a pot on the coals.

Arminian readers hear a judgment that will not be half done, a fire made hot and bones burned, a word the rebellious house is still called to face.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the heaped wood, the hot fire, the well-boiled meat, the thick broth, and the burned bones as the Lord GOD’s appointed completeness of the sign.

Shared ground: the pot is to be boiled through, even to the bones. The cooking image is enough; it is not expanded.

verses.text: Then set it empty on its coals, that it may be hot, and its bronze may burn, and that its filthiness may be molten in it, that its rust may be consumed.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then set it empty on its coals, that it may be hot, and its bronze may burn, and that its filthiness may be molten in it, that its rust may be consumed.” After the pieces are out, the empty pot itself is set on the coals, so that the bronze burns and the rust is consumed. Many readers take this as the city itself, emptied of its people, still under the fire until the stain is gone; the verse describes the empty, rusted bronze on the coals, and that is the sign.

Arminian readers hear a second stage of the parable: not only the contents, but the vessel, are put to the fire, a word that the city’s own uncleanness is not ignored when the people have been taken out.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the empty pot on the coals, the burning bronze, and the rust consumed, as the Lord GOD’s purpose for the vessel itself after the pieces are gone.

Shared ground: the empty cauldron is still on the fire. The rust is to be consumed, as the woe already said it had not gone out.

verses.text: She is weary with toil; yet her great rust, rust by fire, doesn’t leave her.
verses.arminianNotes:
“She is weary with toil; yet her great rust, rust by fire, doesn’t leave her.” The city has labored, and even fire has not yet made the rust leave. The weariness is real, and the stain remains. The line is an indictment, not a riddle about metals.

Arminian readers hear a people worn out by their own toil, and a rust that has still not left, a failure to be clean that the oracle treats as theirs, even under the fire.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same weariness and the great rust that does not leave, even rust by fire, as the Lord GOD’s verdict on a city whose stain remains.

Shared ground: toil has not removed the rust. Both traditions hear that as the city’s unchanged uncleanness.

verses.text: “ ‘ “In your filthiness is lewdness. Because I have cleansed you and you weren’t cleansed, you won’t be cleansed from your filthiness any more, until I have caused my wrath toward you to rest.
verses.arminianNotes:
“In your filthiness is lewdness. Because I have cleansed you and you weren’t cleansed, you won’t be cleansed from your filthiness any more, until I have caused my wrath toward you to rest.” The filthiness is named as lewdness, a moral stain, spoken plainly and without a graphic scene. The LORD says he had cleansed her, and she was not cleansed; cleansing will not come again until his wrath toward her rests.

Arminian readers hear a real prior cleansing that was not received as cleansing, a remaining filthiness that is hers, and a wrath that will rest only when it has done its work, a word still addressed to her as the one who was not cleansed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same lewdness in her filthiness, the cleansing that did not leave her cleansed, and the delay of further cleansing until the LORD’s wrath toward her rests, as his own settled word.

Shared ground: she was not cleansed, and wrath will rest in its time. The traditions can share that indictment without a new dispute over the word “cleansed”.

verses.text: “ ‘ “I, the LORD, have spoken it. It will happen, and I will do it. I won’t go back. I won’t spare. I won’t repent. According to your ways and according to your doings, they will judge you,” says the Lord GOD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
“I, the LORD, have spoken it. It will happen, and I will do it. I won’t go back. I won’t spare. I won’t repent. According to your ways and according to your doings, they will judge you,” says the Lord GOD. The outcome is bound to the word he has spoken. Classical Arminians confess that God knows and will do what he has said, and do not take the future as open or unknown to him. The “I won’t repent” is the certainty of this announced judgment, according to their ways and doings.

Arminian readers hear a word that will stand, a judgment measured to the city’s ways, and a Lord GOD who will not turn back from what he has now spoken.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same “I, the LORD, have spoken it. It will happen, and I will do it.” with no going back, no sparing, and no repenting, as the LORD’s unbreakable resolve, and the judging as according to their ways and doings.

Shared ground: the LORD has spoken, and it will happen. The verse closes the parable with certainty, not with a new contrast over whether God can speak such a word.
